note: Raw findings as each reader returned them. A finding is the reader's claim, not a verified fact; see 2026-11-23-matthew-source-check.md for what was checked.

findings.guideText: Greek and Hebrew forms of the title ‘anointed one,’ carrying royal and other commissioned roles; not Jesus's surname.
findings.evidence: Neither Matthew 1 nor the book briefing defines Christ/Messiah as Greek and Hebrew forms of 'anointed one' or details its royal and commissioned roles (checkable in BDAG/HALOT for χριστός / מָשִׁיחַ).
findings.problem: This concrete claim about the Greek and Hebrew meaning and roles of Christ/Messiah is not supplied by the chapter text or book briefing and names no source, though I believe it is true.

findings.guideText: A legally binding first stage of marriage before the couple began living together; ending it required divorce.
findings.evidence: Matthew 1:18-19 (WEB) uses 'engaged,' 'her husband,' and 'put her away,' and the book briefing does not explain Jewish betrothal law or divorce requirements (checkable in Deut 22:23-24; 24:1 and Mishnah Kiddushin/Ketubot).
findings.problem: This concrete claim about ancient betrothal law and the requirement of divorce to end it is not supplied by the chapter text or book briefing and names no source, though I believe it is true.

findings.guideText: Greek biblos geneseōs can mean a record of origin or genesis and echoes the Greek wording of Genesis.
findings.evidence: Book briefing language.features and language.examples do not mention biblos geneseōs or Genesis; TSK 1:1 lists GEN 2:4 and GEN 5:1 without Greek wording (checkable in LXX Gen 2:4, 5:1).
findings.problem: This concrete claim about the meaning of the Greek phrase biblos geneseōs and its echo of the Greek wording of Genesis is not supplied by the chapter text or book briefing and names no source, though I believe it is true.

findings.guideText: In Hebrew letter-number reckoning, the consonants of David's name can total fourteen, which may reinforce the royal emphasis.
findings.evidence: Neither Matthew 1:17 nor the book briefing (including snags[0]) mentions Hebrew letter-number reckoning or the numerical total of David's name (checkable in standard Hebrew gematria: דוד = 4+6+4 = 14).
findings.problem: This concrete claim about Hebrew letter-number reckoning for David's name is not supplied by the chapter text or book briefing and names no source, though I believe it is true.

findings.guideText: The Greek relative pronoun is feminine singular, pointing to Mary.
findings.evidence: Matthew 1:16 in the hosted WEB reads 'from whom was born Jesus,' and the book briefing does not discuss the Greek relative pronoun in 1:16 (checkable in NA28/SBLGNT Matthew 1:16, ἐξ ἧς).
findings.problem: This concrete claim about the grammatical gender and number of the Greek relative pronoun in 1:16 is not supplied by the chapter text or book briefing and names no source, though I believe it is true.

findings.guideText: ‘you shall name him Jesus, for he will save.’
findings.evidence: Matthew 1:21 (WEB): “She shall give birth to a son. You shall name him Jesus, for it is he who shall save his people from their sins.”
findings.problem: The quoted words alter the hosted WEB text of Matthew 1:21 by omitting 'it is he who' and changing 'shall' to 'will' without ellipsis.

findings.guideText: The Greek expression states what was not true before the birth but does not by itself assert or deny what followed.
findings.evidence: Neither Matthew 1:25 nor the book briefing discusses the Greek expression (ἕως οὗ) or its grammatical usage (checkable in standard Greek grammars for ἕως with the indicative).
findings.problem: This concrete claim about how the Greek expression in 1:25 functions is not supplied by the chapter text or book briefing and names no source, though I believe it is true.

findings.guideText: Greek and Hebrew forms of the title ‘anointed one,’ carrying royal and other commissioned roles; not Jesus's surname.
findings.evidence: The briefing identifies Jesus as Messiah/Christ but does not define the Greek or Hebrew forms as meaning “anointed one”; externally, Greek Christos and Hebrew Mashiach carry that meaning.
findings.problem: I believe this claim is true, but neither the hosted chapter nor the briefing supplies this language claim and the definition names no source.

findings.guideText: A legally binding first stage of marriage before the couple began living together; ending it required divorce.
findings.evidence: Matthew 1:18-19 says Mary was engaged and Joseph intended to put her away, but neither the hosted chapter nor the briefing supplies this full legal definition; externally, Deuteronomy 22:23-24 treats a betrothed woman within marriage law.
findings.problem: I believe this claim is true, but neither the hosted chapter nor the briefing supplies the stated betrothal law and custom and the definition names no source.

findings.guideText: Greek biblos geneseōs can mean a record of origin or genesis and echoes the Greek wording of Genesis.
findings.evidence: Not supplied by Matthew 1 WEB or the book briefing; checkable externally in LXX Genesis 2:4 and 5:1.
findings.problem: I believe this claim is true, but neither the hosted chapter nor the briefing supplies this Greek claim and the sentence names no source.

findings.guideText: In Hebrew letter-number reckoning, the consonants of David's name can total fourteen, which may reinforce the royal emphasis.
findings.evidence: Not supplied by Matthew 1:17 WEB or the book briefing; externally, Hebrew dalet-waw-dalet can be calculated as 4+6+4=14.
findings.problem: I believe this claim is true, but neither the hosted chapter nor the briefing supplies the Hebrew letter-number claim and the sentence names no source.

findings.guideText: The Greek relative pronoun is feminine singular, pointing to Mary.
findings.evidence: Not supplied by Matthew 1:16 WEB or the book briefing; externally, the Greek text has the feminine singular relative form ex hēs.
findings.problem: I believe this claim is true, but neither the hosted chapter nor the briefing supplies this Greek grammatical claim and the sentence names no source.

findings.guideText: Each woman carries an unusual or endangered place in Israel's story, and several are Gentiles or connected with sexual vulnerability.
findings.evidence: Matthew 1:3-6 names the women but does not identify several as Gentiles, and the briefing does not supply those ethnic identities; externally, see Joshua 2 for Rahab and Ruth 1:4 for Ruth as a Moabite.
findings.problem: I believe the Gentile identification is true for at least Rahab and Ruth, but neither the hosted chapter nor the briefing supplies it and the sentence names no source.

findings.guideText: ‘you shall name him Jesus, for he will save.’
findings.evidence: Matthew 1:21 WEB: “You shall name him Jesus, for it is he who shall save his people from their sins.”
findings.problem: The quoted wording rearranges and shortens the hosted verse without an ellipsis.

findings.guideText: The Greek expression states what was not true before the birth but does not by itself assert or deny what followed.
findings.evidence: Not supplied by Matthew 1:25 WEB or the book briefing; externally, this concerns the Greek heōs ou construction in Matthew 1:25.
findings.problem: I believe this claim is true, but neither the hosted chapter nor the briefing supplies this Greek usage claim and the sentence names no source.

findings.guideText: Eastern learned or priestly court figures associated with interpreting stars, dreams, and signs
findings.evidence: Matthew 2:1-2, 12 refers to 'wise men from the east' seeing a star and being warned in a dream, without describing them as priestly court figures; see Herodotus, Histories 1.101, 1.132.
findings.problem: This historical and cultural description of the Magi as priestly court figures is not supplied by the chapter text or book briefing and names no source, though the claim is true.

findings.guideText: known for enormous building projects
findings.evidence: Neither Matthew 2 nor bookBriefing mentions Herod's building projects; see Josephus, Antiquities 15.11.1 (380) and Jewish War 1.21.1 (401).
findings.problem: This historical claim about Herod the Great's building projects is not supplied by the chapter text or book briefing and names no source, though the claim is true.

findings.guideText: Magoi were eastern experts associated with courts, astrology, dreams, or priestly learning.
findings.evidence: Matthew 2:1-2 mentions 'wise men from the east' and 'his star' without the Greek word Magoi or their court/priestly background; see Herodotus, Histories 1.101, 1.132, and Daniel 2:2 (LXX/Theodotion).
findings.problem: The Greek term Magoi and the historical claim about their association with courts, astrology, dreams, or priestly learning are not supplied by the chapter text or book briefing and name no source, though the claim is true.

findings.guideText: three comes from the gifts, while royal imagery grew through later links to Psalms and Isaiah.
findings.evidence: Neither the chapter text nor the book briefing discusses how later tradition developed the 'three kings' imagery from Psalm 72 and Isaiah 60 (though TSK 2:1, 2:11 cross-references those passages).
findings.problem: This historical claim about how later Christian imagery developed is not in the chapter text or book briefing and names no source, though the claim is true.

findings.guideText: Greek proskyneō can describe falling before a ruler, offering homage, or worshiping.
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.language lists Greek terms such as basileia tōn ouranōn, dikaiosynē, and oligopistos, but does not mention proskyneō; see BDAG s.v. προσκυνέω.
findings.problem: This claim about what the Greek word proskyneō means and how it is used is not supplied by the chapter text or book briefing and names no source, though the claim is true.

findings.guideText: play on Hebrew words such as netser (‘branch’)
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.language does not mention Hebrew netser; see Isaiah 11:1 (Hebrew נֵצֶר, nēṣer) and USCCB notes on Matthew 2:23.
findings.problem: This Hebrew language claim is not in the chapter text or book briefing and names no source, though the claim that netser means 'branch' (shoot) is true.

findings.guideText: a Jewish client king
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.whereYouAre mentions 'client rulers' and 'Herod the Great' but does not identify Herod as Jewish; see Josephus, Antiquities 14.15.2 (403) on Herod's Idumean background and rule as king of Judea.
findings.problem: Neither the chapter text nor the book briefing states Herod's ethnic or religious identity as 'Jewish' and no source is named, and the claim is unsure/nuanced because ancient sources describe him as Idumean by descent while practicing Judaism.

findings.guideText: Written after the events; commonly placed in the late first century
findings.evidence: Briefing writtenWhen: “Most current scholarship places the finished Gospel after Mark and after Jerusalem's destruction in AD 70, often in the 80s or 90s. Earlier dates remain defended, so the range is an argument rather than a timestamp supplied by the book.”
findings.problem: The guide drops the briefing’s explicit uncertainty that earlier dates remain defended.

findings.guideText: Eastern learned or priestly court figures associated with interpreting stars, dreams, and signs; not identified as three kings in Matthew.
findings.evidence: MAT 2:1 says “wise men from the east” and MAT 2:11 lists three gifts, but neither the chapter nor the briefing defines magi as learned or priestly court figures.
findings.problem: The definition’s concrete occupational and priestly claims are supplied by neither the chapter nor the briefing and name no source; I believe they are true.

findings.guideText: Rome-backed king of Judea, known for enormous building projects and lethal defense of his rule.
findings.evidence: MAT 2 depicts Herod as king and as ordering killings in 2:16, and the briefing says Rome used client rulers, but neither source supplies Herod’s enormous building projects.
findings.problem: The building-projects claim is a concrete historical claim supplied by neither the chapter nor the briefing and naming no source; I believe it is true.

findings.guideText: modifies the citation to interpret Bethlehem's significance
findings.evidence: MAT 2:6 supplies Matthew’s wording and TSK points to MIC 5:2, but the bundle does not supply Micah’s text or state that Matthew modified the citation; the briefing says only that Matthew’s citations may resemble Septuagint, Hebrew, or mixed forms.
findings.problem: This concrete textual-modification claim is supplied by neither the hosted chapter nor the briefing and names no source; I believe it is true.

findings.guideText: Foreign court experts recognize the king that Herod fears and Jerusalem's interpreters do not visit.
findings.evidence: MAT 2:11 says the wise men worshiped and gave gifts, but neither MAT 2 nor the briefing identifies them as court experts.
findings.problem: The court-expert identification is a concrete historical claim supplied by neither the chapter nor the briefing and naming no source; I believe it is true.

findings.guideText: Magoi were eastern experts associated with courts, astrology, dreams, or priestly learning.
findings.evidence: MAT 2:1 says only “wise men from the east”; the briefing gives no definition of magoi by court role, astrology, dreams, or priestly learning.
findings.problem: This is a concrete language and history claim supplied by neither the chapter nor the briefing and naming no source; I believe it is true.

findings.guideText: royal imagery grew through later links to Psalms and Isaiah
findings.evidence: TSK lists PSA 72 and ISA 60 as comparison routes for MAT 2:1, but TSK matches are not proof of a later interpretive development, and the briefing supplies no such history.
findings.problem: This concrete claim about later interpretation is supplied by neither the chapter nor the briefing and names no source for that development; I believe it is true.

findings.guideText: Greek proskyneō can describe falling before a ruler, offering homage, or worshiping.
findings.evidence: MAT 2:2, 2:8, and 2:11 use “worship” in the hosted English; the briefing’s language features do not include proskyneō or this range of meanings.
findings.problem: This Greek lexical claim is supplied by neither the chapter nor the briefing and names no source; I believe it is true.

findings.guideText: the same verb appears around Jesus's divine authority later
findings.evidence: The briefing does not discuss proskyneō or its later occurrences in Matthew, and MAT 2 supplies only verses 2, 8, and 11.
findings.problem: This concrete cross-chapter Greek-usage claim is supplied by neither this chapter nor the briefing and names no source; I believe it is true.

findings.guideText: This is not an attack on study; it is an early warning that possession of correct words does not guarantee allegiance.
findings.evidence: MAT 2:4-5 shows the chief priests and scribes answering Herod, and MAT 2:9-11 shows the magi traveling and worshiping, but the text does not state this warning as Matthew’s verdict on the scholars.
findings.problem: The guide presents one interpretive and preaching application alone without marking it as a reading or noting that readers differ.

findings.guideText: play on Hebrew words such as netser (‘branch’)
findings.evidence: MAT 2:23 says only “he will be called a Nazarene”; the briefing supplies no Hebrew word netser, its meaning, or a link to Nazarene.
findings.problem: This Hebrew lexical claim is supplied by neither the chapter nor the briefing and names no source; I believe the gloss “branch” is true, while its explanatory link here remains debated.

findings.guideText: Gentile seekers worship while a Jewish client king kills;
findings.evidence: The briefing identifies the magi among Gentiles and says Rome ruled through client rulers, but it does not identify Herod as a Jewish client king; MAT 2 calls him only “King Herod.”
findings.problem: Herod’s identification here as a Jewish client king is a concrete historical claim supplied by neither the chapter nor the briefing and naming no source; I am unsure whether the ethnic label is accurate without qualification.

findings.guideText: Anonymous Gospel narrator using and expanding earlier tradition
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.facts.writtenBy: "Anonymous within the narrative. The ancient title ‘According to Matthew’ and early church testimony connect it with Matthew the tax collector and apostle; the text itself never names its writer." and bookBriefing.debates[0]
findings.problem: The author field presents the anonymous-author view alone and drops the book briefing's uncertainty regarding early church attribution to Matthew the apostle.

findings.guideText: Distinct Jewish movements with different social bases and beliefs;
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.cast (“Different Jewish groups and leaders”); checkable in Josephus, Antiquities 18.1.2–4
findings.problem: True historical claim that Pharisees and Sadducees had different social bases and beliefs, but neither the chapter text nor the book briefing supplies those details and no source is named.

findings.guideText: Metanoeite is a command to change mind and direction
findings.evidence: Not in hostedTranslation or bookBriefing.language.features; checkable in Matthew 3:2 (Greek μετανοεῖτε / metanoeite)
findings.problem: True claim about the Greek verb in Matthew 3:2, but neither the chapter text nor the book briefing supplies this Greek word or its meaning and no source is named.

findings.guideText: Pharisees and Sadducees were distinct movements and often disagreed with each other.
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.cast calls them “Different Jewish groups and leaders,” without stating they often disagreed; checkable in Acts 23:6–9 and Josephus, Antiquities 13.10.6
findings.problem: True historical claim that Pharisees and Sadducees often disagreed with each other, but neither the chapter text nor the book briefing supplies it and no source is named.

findings.guideText: ‘brood of vipers’
findings.evidence: Matthew 3:7 (WEB): “You offspring of vipers, who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?
findings.problem: The question quotes ‘brood of vipers’ as the text, whereas the hosted World English Bible reads “offspring of vipers.”

findings.guideText: Greek baptizō means immerse or wash.
findings.evidence: Not in hostedTranslation or bookBriefing.language.features; checkable in standard Greek lexicons (e.g., BDAG, baptizō)
findings.problem: True Greek lexical claim, but neither the hosted chapter text nor the book briefing supplies baptizō or its meaning and no source is named.

findings.guideText: Jewish life already included many ritual washings,
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.whereYouAre and cast mention “purity” debates, not ritual washings; checkable in Mark 7:3–4 and Second Temple purity practices
findings.problem: True historical/custom claim about Jewish ritual washings, but neither the chapter text nor the book briefing supplies it and no source is named.

findings.guideText: ‘with Holy Spirit and fire’
findings.evidence: Matthew 3:11 (WEB): “He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit.
findings.problem: The question quotes ‘with Holy Spirit and fire’ as the text, whereas the hosted World English Bible reads “in the Holy Spirit” without “and fire.”

findings.guideText: A community familiar with baptism, Scripture, and debates about Abrahamic identity
findings.evidence: Briefing writtenFor: “Greek-speaking readers deeply familiar with Jewish Scripture and debate, probably a community containing Jewish and Gentile followers of Jesus.”
findings.problem: The field drops the briefing’s Greek-speaking and probably Jewish-and-Gentile audience and adds familiarity with baptism, which the briefing does not supply.

findings.guideText: Distinct Jewish movements with different social bases and beliefs; not one uniform ruling group.
findings.evidence: Briefing cast describes Pharisees, Sadducees, scribes, and chief priests only as “Different Jewish groups and leaders, not one interchangeable enemy,” with no account of social bases.
findings.problem: I believe the distinct-movements claim is true, but the specific claim about different social bases is supplied by neither the chapter nor the briefing and names no source.

findings.guideText: Metanoeite is a command to change mind and direction — a reorientation visible in conduct, not merely feeling sorry.
findings.evidence: BDAG s.v. metanoeō supports the gloss, but the briefing’s language features and examples contain no metanoeō/metanoeite entry.
findings.problem: I believe the claim is true, but neither the chapter nor the briefing supplies this Greek meaning and the sentence names no source.

findings.guideText: Greek baptizō means immerse or wash.
findings.evidence: BDAG s.v. baptizō supports the gloss, but the briefing’s language features and examples contain no baptizō entry.
findings.problem: I believe the claim is true, but neither the chapter nor the briefing supplies this Greek meaning and the sentence names no source.

findings.guideText: Jewish life already included many ritual washings, but John's one-time prophetic action in the Jordan carries an end-time urgency and prepares for one who will act with the Holy Spirit.
findings.evidence: Ritual washing is attested in texts such as Leviticus 15 and later miqveh practice, but neither Matthew 3:6,11 nor the briefing supplies that background or a one-time contrast.
findings.problem: I believe the ritual-washing background is broadly true, but it is a history/custom claim supplied by neither source and the sentence names no source.

findings.guideText: Does baptism ‘with Holy Spirit and fire’ promise blessing or judgment?
findings.evidence: MAT 3:11 hosted text: “He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit.”
findings.problem: The hosted verse does not contain “and fire,” so the quoted phrase is not the hosted chapter text.

findings.guideText: Jesus answers that the act is fitting ‘to fulfill all righteousness’: he identifies with the people and enacts the Father's will before being commissioned.
findings.evidence: MAT 3:15 hosted text: “Allow it now, for this is the fitting way for us to fulfill all righteousness.”
findings.problem: The verse does not state identification with the people as the reason, so this gives one interpretive reading alone without identifying it as a reading.

findings.guideText: The words combine royal and servant language: Psalm 2 speaks to God's anointed Son, while Isaiah 42 introduces the servant in whom God delights and on whom the Spirit rests.
findings.evidence: MAT 3:17 hosted text: “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased”; TSK 3:17 lists PSA 2:7 and ISA 42:1 only as comparison routes.
findings.problem: The combined Psalm 2/Isaiah 42 echo is presented as settled rather than as one reading, although TSK matches are not proof that the texts mean the same thing.

findings.guideText: Anonymous Greek narrator arranging scriptural testing and ministry scenes
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.facts.writtenBy: "Anonymous within the narrative. The ancient title ‘According to Matthew’ and early church testimony connect it with Matthew the tax collector and apostle; the text itself never names its writer."
findings.problem: The author field presents an anonymous Greek narrator as settled fact and drops the book briefing's uncertainty between traditional attribution to Matthew and an anonymous Greek-speaking Jewish-Christian writer.

findings.guideText: Late-first-century composition narrating the beginning of Jesus's Galilean ministry
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.facts.writtenWhen: "Most current scholarship places the finished Gospel after Mark and after Jerusalem's destruction in AD 70, often in the 80s or 90s. Earlier dates remain defended, so the range is an argument rather than a timestamp supplied by the book."
findings.problem: The date field states a late-first-century composition without preserving the book briefing's note that earlier dates remain defended and that the date range is an argument rather than a supplied timestamp.

findings.guideText: Wilderness, then Galilee around Capernaum under Herod Antipas
findings.evidence: Matthew 4:12 and bookBriefing.whereYouAre (neither names Herod Antipas)
findings.problem: Naming Herod Antipas as the ruler of Galilee is a true historical claim that neither the chapter text nor the book briefing supplies and for which no source is named.

findings.guideText: Greek and Semitic designations for the slanderer or adversary who tests Jesus's allegiance.
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.language.examples (does not include diabolos or satanas)
findings.problem: Defining Devil and Satan as Greek and Semitic designations for slanderer or adversary is a true linguistic claim that neither the chapter text nor the book briefing supplies and for which no source is named.

findings.evidence: Matthew 4:15 ("Galilee of the Gentiles") and bookBriefing (does not describe Galilee's conquest history)
findings.problem: Describing Galilee of the Gentiles as a northern border region shaped by conquest and mixed populations is a true historical and geographical claim that neither the chapter text nor the book briefing supplies and for which no source is named.

findings.guideText: Greek peirazō can mean test or tempt; context supplies the moral direction.
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.language.features (does not mention peirazō)
findings.problem: Stating what the Greek verb peirazō can mean is a true linguistic claim that neither the chapter text nor the book briefing supplies and for which no source is named.

findings.guideText: The Greek condition can work as ‘if, as claimed,’ not necessarily uncertainty.
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.language (does not discuss Greek conditional clauses)
findings.problem: Stating how the Greek conditional construction works is a true linguistic claim that neither the chapter text nor the book briefing supplies and for which no source is named.

findings.guideText: Euangelion means good news or royal announcement, not yet a bound book called a Gospel.
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.language (does not mention euangelion)
findings.problem: Stating what the Greek word euangelion means is a true linguistic claim that neither the chapter text nor the book briefing supplies and for which no source is named.

findings.guideText: Late-first-century composition narrating the beginning of Jesus's Galilean ministry
findings.evidence: Briefing facts.writtenWhen: 'Most current scholarship places the finished Gospel after Mark and after Jerusalem's destruction in AD 70, often in the 80s or 90s. Earlier dates remain defended, so the range is an argument rather than a timestamp supplied by the book.'
findings.problem: The guide states a late-first-century date as settled and drops the briefing's stated uncertainty about earlier dates.

findings.guideText: Wilderness, then Galilee around Capernaum under Herod Antipas
findings.evidence: MAT 4:12-13 says only that John was 'delivered up,' Jesus 'withdrew into Galilee' and 'lived in Capernaum'; briefing whereYouAre names Rome's governors and client rulers and Herod the Great for the opening, not Herod Antipas (cf. Josephus, Antiquities 18, for Antipas ruling Galilee).
findings.problem: I believe the Herod Antipas claim is true, but neither the chapter text nor the briefing supplies it and the sentence names no source.

findings.guideText: Greek and Semitic designations for the slanderer or adversary who tests Jesus's allegiance.
findings.evidence: MAT 4 uses 'the devil' (4:1) and 'Satan' (4:10) in English; briefing language.examples lists Iēsous, Emmanouēl, rhaka, mamōnas, hōsanna and the 27:46 cry, but gives no meanings for diabolos or Satan (cf. BDAG, diabolos and Satanas).
findings.problem: I believe the claim is true, but it is a language claim supplied by neither the chapter text nor the briefing and the sentence names no source.

findings.guideText: Isaiah's description of a northern border region shaped by conquest and mixed populations; Matthew frames Jesus's Galilean work as light.
findings.evidence: MAT 4:14-16 says only that it was 'spoken through Isaiah the prophet' and quotes 'The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, toward the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles'; neither text nor briefing mentions conquest or mixed populations (cf. 2 Kings 15:29 for the Assyrian conquest of the region).
findings.problem: I believe the claim is broadly true, but the conquest and mixed-population history is supplied by neither the chapter text nor the briefing and the sentence names no source.

findings.guideText: Good news or royal announcement before it became the name for a written Jesus narrative.
findings.evidence: MAT 4:23 reads 'preaching the Good News of the Kingdom'; briefing form describes Matthew as a 'Gospel' but gives no history of euangelion becoming a book title (cf. BDAG, euangelion).
findings.problem: I believe the claim is true, but it is a Greek-language and usage-history claim supplied by neither the chapter text nor the briefing and the sentence names no source.

findings.guideText: Greek peirazō can mean test or tempt; context supplies the moral direction.
findings.evidence: Briefing language.features and language.examples list Greek terms such as basileia tōn ouranōn, dikaiosynē and oligopistos, but not peirazō (cf. BDAG, peirazō, 'test/tempt').
findings.problem: I believe the claim is true, but it is a Greek-language claim supplied by neither the chapter text nor the briefing and the sentence names no source.

findings.evidence: MAT 4:3 and 4:6 in the hosted text read 'If you are the Son of God'; briefing language material gives no rule for Greek conditional clauses (cf. a Greek grammar on first-class conditions, e.g. Smyth §§2244-46).
findings.problem: I believe the claim is true, but it is a Greek-language claim supplied by neither the chapter text nor the briefing and the sentence names no source.

findings.guideText: Euangelion means good news or royal announcement, not yet a bound book called a Gospel.
findings.evidence: MAT 4:23 in the hosted text reads 'preaching the Good News of the Kingdom'; briefing language.features and language.examples do not discuss euangelion or its usage history (cf. BDAG, euangelion).
findings.problem: I believe the claim is true, but it is a Greek-language and usage claim supplied by neither the chapter text nor the briefing and the sentence names no source.

findings.guideText: Late-first-century Gospel preserving and arranging earlier teaching
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.facts.writtenWhen: Most current scholarship places the finished Gospel after Mark and after Jerusalem's destruction in AD 70, often in the 80s or 90s. Earlier dates remain defended, so the range is an argument rather than a timestamp supplied by the book.
findings.problem: The context date states a late-first-century date as settled fact and drops the briefing's explicit caveat that earlier dates remain defended.

findings.guideText: A name derived from Jerusalem's Valley of Hinnom that became an image of divine judgment.
findings.evidence: 2 Kings 23:10 / Jeremiah 7:31-32 and Second Temple Jewish usage (e.g. BDAG, s.v. γέεννα); neither the chapter text nor bookBriefing mentions the Valley of Hinnom or Gehenna's background.
findings.problem: This makes an unsourced geographical and linguistic claim about Gehenna that is not supplied by the chapter text or book briefing (claim is true).

findings.guideText: Makarios names someone fortunate or in an enviable position because of God's favor and promised future, even when present feeling is grief or persecution.
findings.evidence: Greek lexicon (e.g. BDAG, s.v. μακάριος); neither the Greek word makarios nor its definition appears in the chapter text or bookBriefing.
findings.problem: This makes an unsourced factual claim about what the Greek word makarios means that is not supplied by the chapter text or book briefing (claim is true).

findings.guideText: Luke's parallel says simply ‘poor.’
findings.evidence: Luke 6:20; TSK lists LUK 6:20 as a cross-reference for 5:3, but neither the chapter text nor bookBriefing supplies Luke's wording.
findings.problem: This states what another ancient text says without naming a chapter-and-verse source and without the wording appearing in the grounding bundle (claim is true).

findings.guideText: Gehenna comes from the Valley of Hinnom near Jerusalem and had become an image of divine judgment.
findings.evidence: 2 Kings 23:10 / Jeremiah 7:31-32 and Second Temple Jewish usage (e.g. BDAG, s.v. γέεννα); neither the chapter text nor bookBriefing mentions the Valley of Hinnom or Gehenna's background.

findings.evidence: Matthew 13:29 says only, 'lest perhaps while you gather up the darnel weeds, you root up the wheat with them'; neither that verse nor the briefing supplies early resemblance to wheat or intertwining roots.
findings.problem: I believe this claim is true for darnel, but the botanical resemblance and root claims are unsourced and unsupported by the chapter or briefing.

findings.guideText: The lesson checks communities eager to purify the world by force; it does not forbid all accountability, which chapter 18 will address.
findings.evidence: Matthew 13:38-39 identifies the field as the world and the harvest as the end of the age with angels as reapers, and 13:30 defers sorting to that harvest, while the guide applies the parable to present community accountability without marking it as one reading or noting that readers differ.
findings.problem: The guide presents one contested present-day community application of the wheat-and-weeds parable as the settled lesson without signalling that it is a reading.

findings.guideText: Both can carry suspicious associations — invasive mustard and fermenting yeast — yet here they picture astonishing growth and permeation from something hidden and small.
findings.evidence: Matthew 13:31-33 likens the kingdom to a mustard seed and to yeast hidden in meal but supplies no suspicious, invasive, or fermenting associations, and neither does the briefing.
findings.problem: I am unsure whether both association claims are true as stated, and they are unsourced historical-cultural claims unsupported by the chapter or briefing.

findings.guideText: Late-first-century Gospel composition
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.facts.writtenWhen: "Most current scholarship places the finished Gospel after Mark and after Jerusalem's destruction in AD 70, often in the 80s or 90s. Earlier dates remain defended, so the range is an argument rather than a timestamp supplied by the book."
findings.problem: Stating a late-first-century date without qualification drops the briefing's explicit note that earlier dates remain defended and that the range is an argument rather than a fact supplied by the book.

findings.guideText: Rome-supported ruler of Galilee and Perea, son of Herod the Great and executor of John.
findings.evidence: Matthew 14:1 says "Herod the tetrarch" and bookBriefing.whereYouAre mentions "Herod the Great" without identifying Herod Antipas or Perea; checkable in Josephus, Antiquities 17.8.1 and 18.5.2.
findings.problem: This historical identification is true, but neither the chapter text nor the book briefing supplies the name Antipas, his rule over Galilee and Perea, or his parentage, and no source is named.

findings.guideText: Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ruled Galilee under Rome.
findings.evidence: Matthew 14:1 calls him "Herod the tetrarch" without naming Antipas, Herod the Great, or Galilee; checkable in Luke 3:1 and Josephus, Antiquities 17.8.1.
findings.problem: This claim is true, but neither Matthew 14 nor the book briefing supplies Herod's name Antipas, his parentage, or that he ruled Galilee, and no source is named.

findings.guideText: Guilt and popular speculation make Jesus's works sound to him like the return of the prophet he executed.
findings.evidence: Matthew 14:1-2: "At that time, Herod the tetrarch heard the report concerning Jesus, and said to his servants, 'This is John the Baptizer. He is risen from the dead. That is why these powers work in him.'"
findings.problem: The hosted text records Herod's statement without stating that guilt or popular speculation caused it, so presenting that motive as flat fact rather than one reading overreaches the text.

findings.guideText: Splagchnizomai comes from language for the inward organs, the felt seat of deep emotion.
findings.evidence: Matthew 14:14 uses "had compassion" and bookBriefing.language does not mention splagchnizomai; checkable in BDAG / LSJ s.v. splagchnizomai.
findings.problem: This claim about Greek vocabulary is true, but neither the chapter text nor the book briefing supplies the word splagchnizomai or its etymology, and no source is named.

findings.guideText: Greek egō eimi can be ordinary self-identification — ‘it is I’ — and can also carry scriptural resonance when spoken by one walking the chaotic sea and saying ‘do not fear.’
findings.evidence: Matthew 14:27 has "It is I!" and bookBriefing.language does not mention egō eimi; checkable in the Greek New Testament (Matt 14:27) and BDAG s.v. eimi.
findings.problem: This claim about Greek phrasing and usage is true, but neither the chapter text nor the book briefing supplies egō eimi or its range of meaning, and no source is named.

findings.guideText: Distazō suggests wavering or being divided between alternatives.
findings.evidence: Matthew 14:31 has "why did you doubt?" and bookBriefing.language does not mention distazō; checkable in the Greek New Testament (Matt 14:31) and BDAG s.v. distazō.
findings.problem: This claim about Greek vocabulary is true, but neither the chapter text nor the book briefing supplies the word distazō or its meaning, and no source is named.

findings.guideText: Readers learning to recognize messianic authority without hiding disciple failure
findings.evidence: Briefing writtenFor: “Greek-speaking readers deeply familiar with Jewish Scripture and debate, probably a community containing Jewish and Gentile followers of Jesus.”
findings.problem: The guide replaces the briefing's audience and drops its probable, mixed-community description.

findings.guideText: Late-first-century Gospel composition
findings.evidence: Briefing writtenWhen: “Most current scholarship places the finished Gospel after Mark and after Jerusalem's destruction in AD 70, often in the 80s or 90s. Earlier dates remain defended, so the range is an argument rather than a timestamp supplied by the book.”
findings.problem: The guide states a late date flatly and drops the briefing's uncertainty about earlier defended dates.

findings.guideText: Flashback martyrdom, feeding sign, sea theophany, and healing summary
findings.evidence: Briefing form.name: “Gospel — an ancient life-of-a-person arranged as scriptural narrative, teaching, controversy, passion, and commission.”
findings.problem: The guide replaces the briefing's Gospel form with episode labels, including the interpretive label theophany, without preserving the book-level form.

findings.guideText: Rome-supported ruler of Galilee and Perea, son of Herod the Great and executor of John.
findings.evidence: MAT 14:1 calls him “Herod the tetrarch” and MAT 14:10 says John was beheaded at his command; Galilee and Perea as Antipas's tetrarchy are checkable in Josephus, Antiquities 18.2.1, but sonship, Perea, and Rome-supported rule are supplied by neither the chapter nor the briefing.
findings.problem: I believe the claim is true, but it repeats unsourced history and geography claims that the grounding does not supply.

findings.guideText: Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ruled Galilee under Rome.
findings.evidence: MAT 14:1 calls him only “Herod the tetrarch”; the identity and rule are checkable in Josephus, Antiquities 18.2.1, but are supplied by neither the chapter text nor the briefing.
findings.problem: I believe the claim is true, but it is an unsourced history claim that the grounding does not supply.

findings.guideText: Guilt and popular speculation make Jesus's works sound to him like the return of the prophet he executed.
findings.evidence: MAT 14:2: Herod “said to his servants, “This is John the Baptizer. He is risen from the dead””; MAT 14:5 says he feared the multitude because they counted John as a prophet, with no statement of guilt or popular speculation about Jesus.
findings.problem: The guide invents Herod's motive and attributes the identification to popular speculation with certainty the chapter does not give.

findings.guideText: His oath is made publicly before banquet guests, and honor culture turns retreat into loss of face.
findings.evidence: MAT 14:9 gives only “for the sake of his oaths and of those who sat at the table with him”; no honor-culture or loss-of-face explanation is supplied by the chapter or briefing.
findings.problem: I believe the broad honor-culture claim is true, but its application here is an unsourced custom claim.

findings.guideText: Splagchnizomai comes from language for the inward organs, the felt seat of deep emotion.
findings.evidence: MAT 14:14 hosted text reads “He had compassion on them”; the Greek etymology is checkable under BDAG splanchna/splanchnizomai but is not among the briefing's language features for this verse.
findings.problem: I believe the claim is true, but it is an unsourced Greek-language claim outside the supplied grounding.

findings.guideText: Greek egō eimi can be ordinary self-identification — ‘it is I’ — and can also carry scriptural resonance when spoken by one walking the chaotic sea and saying ‘do not fear.’
findings.evidence: MAT 14:27 hosted text reads “It is I! Don’t be afraid.”; the Greek phrase and its range are not supplied in the briefing's language features.
findings.problem: I believe the claim is true, but it is an unsourced Greek-language claim outside the supplied grounding, even though it is hedged.

findings.guideText: Distazō suggests wavering or being divided between alternatives.
findings.evidence: MAT 14:31 hosted text reads “why did you doubt?”; BDAG distazō supports the gloss, but the briefing's 14:31 feature covers oligopistos only and does not supply distazō.
findings.problem: I believe the claim is true, but it is an unsourced Greek-language claim outside the supplied grounding.

findings.guideText: Mixed communities negotiating Jewish practice, Gentile inclusion, and table fellowship
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.facts.writtenFor ("probably a community containing Jewish and Gentile followers of Jesus") and bookBriefing.debates[1] (listing three positions: Jewish follower-of-Jesus community, mixed community, and predominantly Gentile church)
findings.problem: The guide states a mixed community as settled fact, dropping the book briefing's "probably" and the ongoing scholarly debate over Matthew's audience and relationship to Judaism.

findings.guideText: Late-first-century Gospel composition
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.facts.writtenWhen ("Most current scholarship places the finished Gospel after Mark and after Jerusalem's destruction in AD 70, often in the 80s or 90s. Earlier dates remain defended, so the range is an argument rather than a timestamp supplied by the book.")
findings.problem: The guide presents a late-first-century date without preserving the book briefing's caveat that earlier dates remain defended and that the date is an argument rather than a timestamp.

findings.guideText: Such traditions extended priestly holiness into daily life.
findings.evidence: Matthew 15:2 refers to "the tradition of the elders" regarding handwashing before eating bread, and the book briefing does not discuss priestly holiness or the origin of mealtime handwashing (general Second Temple historical scholarship).
findings.problem: This historical claim about the origin and purpose of handwashing traditions is not supplied by the chapter text or book briefing and names no source; I believe the claim is generally true as a scholarly view, though its details are debated.

findings.guideText: Matthew does not preserve the Semitic term that Mark explains, but the logic is the same: religious speech shields someone from a direct obligation.
findings.evidence: Matthew 15:5 ("a gift devoted to God") does not name Corban, and the book briefing does not mention Corban or Mark's explanation of it (Mark 7:11).
findings.problem: The reference to "the Semitic term that Mark explains" (along with "Corban-like" in questions[1].question) relies on Mark 7:11, which is not in Matthew 15 or the book briefing and is not cited; I believe the claim is true.

findings.guideText: Matthew does not add Mark's editorial phrase often translated ‘declaring all foods clean.’
findings.evidence: Matthew 15:17-20 and the book briefing do not supply the wording of Mark 7:19 ("declaring all foods clean").
findings.problem: This factual claim about what Mark's parallel passage includes is not in the chapter text or the book briefing and names no specific Markan reference; I believe the claim is true.

findings.guideText: In biblical usage kardia is the center of thought, intention, desire, and will, not emotion alone.
findings.evidence: Matthew 15:18-19 uses "heart" without discussing the Greek word kardia, and bookBriefing.language does not list or define kardia (standard Greek lexicography).
findings.problem: This Greek lexical claim about kardia is not supplied by the chapter text or the book briefing and names no source; I believe the claim is true.

findings.guideText: ‘Canaanite’ is an archaic, scripturally charged identity for Israel's ancient outsiders; Mark calls the woman Syrophoenician.
findings.evidence: Matthew 15:22 calls her "a Canaanite woman" without explaining the term's archaic scriptural background or Mark 7:26 ("Syrophoenician"), and the book briefing does not supply either claim.
findings.problem: Both the historical-literary characterization of "Canaanite" and the claim about Mark's wording are absent from the chapter text and book briefing and name no source; I believe both claims are true.

findings.guideText: the diminutive kynaria refers to household dogs
findings.evidence: Matthew 15:26-27 reads "dogs" in the hosted WEB, and bookBriefing.language does not discuss kynaria (standard Greek lexicography / Greek text of Matthew 15:26-27).
findings.problem: This Greek grammatical and lexical claim about the diminutive kynaria is not in the hosted text or the book briefing and names no source; I believe the claim is true.

findings.guideText: Mixed communities negotiating Jewish practice, Gentile inclusion, and table fellowship
findings.evidence: Briefing writtenFor: “Greek-speaking readers deeply familiar with Jewish Scripture and debate, probably a community containing Jewish and Gentile followers of Jesus.”
findings.problem: The guide presents a probable mixed community as settled and adds table-fellowship negotiation that the briefing does not state.

findings.guideText: Late-first-century Gospel composition

findings.problem: The guide drops the briefing’s uncertainty and the earlier dates that remain defended.

findings.guideText: Interpretive practices handed down to apply Torah to daily life; Jesus disputes misuse, not the existence of interpretation.
findings.evidence: Matthew 15:2-3 names “the tradition of the elders” and “your tradition” but does not define it as practices applying Torah to daily life; the briefing supplies no such definition.
findings.problem: I believe this description of the tradition is true, but neither the chapter text nor the briefing supplies it and the definition names no source.

findings.guideText: Such traditions extended priestly holiness into daily life.
findings.evidence: Matthew 15:2 says only that the disciples “don’t wash their hands when they eat bread” under “the tradition of the elders”; the briefing discusses disagreement about purity but does not describe an extension of priestly holiness into daily meals.
findings.problem: I believe this historical claim about handwashing practice is true, but neither the chapter text nor the briefing supplies it and the sentence names no source.

findings.guideText: In biblical usage kardia is the center of thought, intention, desire, and will, not emotion alone.
findings.evidence: Matthew 15:18-19 in the hosted WEB says “heart” without any Greek lexical note; the briefing’s language features and examples supply no entry for kardia (checkable in BDAG under καρδία).
findings.problem: I believe this Greek lexical claim is true, but neither the chapter text nor the briefing supplies it and the sentence names no source.

findings.guideText: ‘Canaanite’ is an archaic, scripturally charged identity for Israel's ancient outsiders
findings.evidence: Matthew 15:22 calls her only “a Canaanite woman”; the briefing’s cast list mentions “the Canaanite woman” but gives no history of the term as archaic or scripturally charged.
findings.problem: I believe this historical and language claim is true, but neither the chapter text nor the briefing supplies it and the clause names no source.

findings.guideText: The image prioritizes Israel's children, and the diminutive kynaria refers to household dogs, but softening the noun does not erase the unequal comparison.
findings.evidence: Matthew 15:26 in the hosted WEB says only “dogs”; the briefing’s language features and examples supply no entry for kynaria (checkable in BDAG under κυνάριον).
findings.problem: I believe the Greek diminutive claim is true, but neither the chapter text nor the briefing supplies it and the sentence names no source.

findings.guideText: In a context moving through Gentile-associated territory, the second scene displays provision again while disciples again ask where bread could come from.
findings.evidence: Matthew 15:29 locates the feeding only “near to the sea of Galilee” on “the mountain,” and 15:31 says the crowd “glorified the God of Israel”; neither verse nor the briefing identifies the feeding scene’s territory as Gentile-associated.
findings.problem: I am unsure whether the feeding scene should be classified as Gentile-associated territory, and in any case neither the chapter text nor the briefing supplies that classification and the sentence names no source.

findings.guideText: Repetition is the point, not an editing accident to be hurried past.
findings.evidence: Matthew 15:32-37 narrates the second feeding without stating its purpose; the briefing’s shape note for chapters 14–18 lists “Bread, water, purity, a Canaanite woman's persistence” without settling why the feeding is repeated.
findings.problem: The guide presents one literary reading as settled and dismisses an alternative editorial explanation without marking it as a reading.

findings.guideText: In Gentile territory a Canaanite woman persists through silence, an Israel-focused mission saying, and a household-dog image until Jesus praises her great faith.
findings.evidence: Matthew 15:21 says only that Jesus “withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon”; neither that verse nor the book briefing classifies the region as Gentile territory.
findings.problem: I believe the geographical classification is true, but neither the chapter text nor the briefing supplies it and the sentence names no source.

findings.guideText: Late-first-century Gospel composition
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.facts.writtenWhen: "Most current scholarship places the finished Gospel after Mark and after Jerusalem's destruction in AD 70, often in the 80s or 90s. Earlier dates remain defended, so the range is an argument rather than a timestamp supplied by the book."
findings.problem: The guide's date field drops the book briefing's explicit note that earlier dates remain defended and that the range is an argument rather than a settled timestamp.

findings.guideText: Galilee and the Gentile-associated district around Caesarea Philippi
findings.evidence: MAT 16:13 ("the parts of Caesarea Philippi"); bookBriefing does not describe Caesarea Philippi as Gentile-associated.
findings.problem: Neither the hosted chapter text nor the book briefing supplies the geographical and historical claim that the district around Caesarea Philippi was Gentile-associated, and no source is named (true).

findings.guideText: Hebrew and Greek forms of ‘anointed one,’ especially a royal title in this scene.
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.language does not supply the meaning or etymology of Messiah and Christ as Hebrew and Greek forms of "anointed one."
findings.problem: The glossary makes a Hebrew and Greek language claim that neither the chapter text nor the book briefing supplies and names no source (true).

findings.guideText: The realm of the dead; ‘gates’ picture death's power, not demons attacking from an entrance.
findings.evidence: MAT 16:18 ("gates of Hades"); bookBriefing does not define Hades.
findings.problem: The glossary defines the Greek term "Hades" as "The realm of the dead" without support from the chapter text or book briefing and names no source (true).

findings.guideText: Christos is Greek for ‘anointed one,’ corresponding to Messiah.
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.language does not list Christos or define it as Greek for "anointed one" corresponding to Messiah.
findings.problem: The guide makes a Greek lexical claim about Christos that neither the chapter text nor the book briefing supplies and names no source (true).

findings.guideText: Greek has Petros for Peter and petra for rock; Jesus likely spoke an Aramaic form kepha that could serve both name and rock.
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.language does not mention Petros, petra, or Aramaic kepha.
findings.problem: The guide makes Greek and Aramaic language claims (Petros, petra, kepha) that neither the chapter text nor the book briefing supplies and names no source (true).

findings.guideText: and can echo the assembly of God's people in Greek Scripture.
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.snags[4] states that Greek ekklēsia means an assembly or gathered community, without mentioning its usage in Greek Scripture.
findings.problem: The claim about how ekklēsia is used in Greek Scripture is a language usage claim not supplied by the chapter text or book briefing and names no source (true).

findings.guideText: binding and loosing can describe forbidding and permitting through interpretation, and later include communal discipline and forgiveness. Greek future-perfect-style wording can be rendered ‘will have been bound in heaven,’
findings.evidence: MAT 16:19 ("will have been bound in heaven"); neither the chapter text nor bookBriefing supplies the Jewish interpretive custom of binding and loosing or the Greek future-perfect grammatical claim.
findings.problem: The guide makes claims about ancient Jewish legal-interpretive custom (forbidding and permitting) and Greek grammar (future-perfect-style wording) that neither the chapter text nor the book briefing supplies and names no source (true).

findings.guideText: Satan means adversary.
findings.evidence: MAT 16:23 ("Get behind me, Satan!"); bookBriefing does not define the word Satan.
findings.problem: The guide makes a lexical claim about the meaning of "Satan" that neither the chapter text nor the book briefing supplies and names no source (true).

findings.guideText: Church communities debating authority, identity, suffering, and faithful interpretation
findings.evidence: Briefing facts.writtenFor: 'Greek-speaking readers deeply familiar with Jewish Scripture and debate, probably a community containing Jewish and Gentile followers of Jesus.'
findings.problem: The guide replaces the briefing's audience description with an unsupported church-communities description.

findings.guideText: Anonymous narrator expanding Peter's confession and marking a major transition
findings.evidence: Briefing facts.writtenBy: 'Anonymous within the narrative. The ancient title ‘According to Matthew’ and early church testimony connect it with Matthew the tax collector and apostle; the text itself never names its writer.'
findings.problem: The briefing supports anonymity but not the claim that the narrator is expanding Peter's confession.

findings.guideText: Late-first-century Gospel composition
findings.evidence: Briefing facts.writtenWhen: 'Most current scholarship places the finished Gospel after Mark and after Jerusalem's destruction in AD 70, often in the 80s or 90s. Earlier dates remain defended, so the range is an argument rather than a timestamp supplied by the book.'
findings.problem: The guide drops the briefing's dating uncertainty and defended earlier dates.

findings.guideText: Galilee and the Gentile-associated district around Caesarea Philippi
findings.evidence: MAT 16:13: 'Now when Jesus came into the parts of Caesarea Philippi'; Nave match for CAESAREA PHILIPPI says only 'A city in the north of Palestine; visited by Jesus.'
findings.problem: Neither the chapter text nor the briefing describes Caesarea Philippi as a Gentile-associated district or locates the opening scenes in Galilee.

findings.guideText: Hebrew and Greek forms of ‘anointed one,’ especially a royal title in this scene.
findings.evidence: The briefing language features and Semitic examples contain no Messiah/Christos entry; MAT 16:16 supplies only the title in Peter's confession.
findings.problem: This Hebrew and Greek language claim is supplied by neither the chapter text nor the briefing and names no source; I believe the claim is true.

findings.guideText: The realm of the dead; ‘gates’ picture death's power, not demons attacking from an entrance.
findings.evidence: MAT 16:18 supplies only 'the gates of Hades will not prevail against it'; the briefing contains no Hades entry defining it as the realm of the dead.
findings.problem: The definition of Hades is supplied by neither the chapter text nor the briefing and names no source; I believe the realm-of-the-dead claim is true.

findings.guideText: The problem is not evidence-seeking itself but a posture that keeps moving the standard after abundant evidence.
findings.evidence: MAT 16:1: 'The Pharisees and Sadducees came, and testing him, asked him to show them a sign from heaven.' MAT 16:3-4 calls them unable to discern the signs of the times but does not describe them moving a standard.
findings.problem: The guide invents a specific motive for the leaders that the text does not state and presents that reading without marking it as a reading.

findings.guideText: Christos is Greek for ‘anointed one,’ corresponding to Messiah.
findings.evidence: Briefing language features and examples contain no Christos/Messiah entry; checkable in standard Greek lexica under χριστός.
findings.problem: This Greek-language claim is supplied by neither the chapter text nor the briefing and names no source; I believe the claim is true.

findings.guideText: In this setting it carries royal and end-time hope, not Jesus's surname.
findings.evidence: MAT 16:16 supplies only 'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God'; the briefing supplies no royal or end-time semantic history for the title.
findings.problem: This historical and linguistic claim about the title's associations is unsupported by the grounding and names no source; I believe the claim is broadly true but simplified.

findings.guideText: Greek has Petros for Peter and petra for rock;
findings.evidence: MAT 16:18 in the hosted text reads 'you are Peter, and on this rock'; the briefing contains no Petros/petra language entry.
findings.problem: This Greek word claim is supplied by neither the hosted text nor the briefing and names no source; I believe the claim is true.

findings.guideText: Jesus likely spoke an Aramaic form kepha that could serve both name and rock.
findings.evidence: Briefing language.spokenWorld: 'the exact spoken language behind an individual scene cannot be recovered merely by translating that Greek backward.'
findings.problem: The guide asserts a likely Aramaic wording behind the scene despite the briefing's explicit caution against recovering it that way.

findings.guideText: Ekklēsia means assembly or gathered community and can echo the assembly of God's people in Greek Scripture.
findings.evidence: Briefing snags support only 'Greek ekklēsia means an assembly or gathered community'; no briefing line supplies the claimed echo of the assembly of God's people in Greek Scripture.
findings.problem: The Greek-Scripture echo claim goes beyond the briefing and names no source; I believe the claim is true but it is not grounded here.

findings.guideText: Keys symbolize stewardly authority; binding and loosing can describe forbidding and permitting through interpretation, and later include communal discipline and forgiveness.
findings.evidence: MAT 16:19 supplies only 'I will give to you the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will have been bound in heaven; and whatever you release on earth will have been released in heaven.'
findings.problem: These claims about the customary and later meanings of keys, binding, and loosing are supplied by neither the chapter text nor the briefing and name no source; I believe they are broadly true.

findings.guideText: Greek future-perfect-style wording can be rendered ‘will have been bound in heaven,’ stressing alignment with heavenly decision.
findings.evidence: The briefing contains no entry on the Greek tense or construction in MAT 16:19; the hosted verse alone supplies the English rendering.
findings.problem: This Greek grammatical claim is supplied by neither the chapter text nor the briefing and names no source; I am unsure the future-perfect description is the right grammatical label.

findings.guideText: Traditions disagree about succession and scope, but the authority is accountable, not autonomous.
findings.evidence: MAT 16:19: 'whatever you bind on earth will have been bound in heaven; and whatever you release on earth will have been released in heaven.'
findings.problem: After noting disagreement, the guide settles the accountability question with a verdict the verse does not state.

findings.guideText: Satan means adversary.
findings.evidence: MAT 16:23 supplies only 'Get behind me, Satan!'; the briefing language section contains no Satan entry.
findings.problem: This Hebrew/Greek language claim is supplied by neither the chapter text nor the briefing and names no source; I believe the claim is true.

findings.guideText: Late-first-century Gospel composition
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.facts.writtenWhen: "Most current scholarship places the finished Gospel after Mark and after Jerusalem's destruction in AD 70, often in the 80s or 90s. Earlier dates remain defended, so the range is an argument rather than a timestamp supplied by the book."
findings.problem: States a late-first-century date without preserving the book briefing's uncertainty that earlier dates remain defended.

findings.guideText: A coin worth approximately the temple-tax payment for two people in the story.
findings.evidence: Matthew 17:24-27 ("didrachma", "stater coin") and bookBriefing (no mention of the temple tax).
findings.problem: Makes an unsourced monetary and customary claim identifying the stater with the temple-tax payment, which neither the chapter text nor the book briefing supplies; I believe the claim is true.

findings.evidence: Matthew 17:27 ("stumble") and bookBriefing.language (no mention of scandalizō).
findings.problem: Makes an unsourced Greek lexical claim not supplied by the chapter text or book briefing; I believe the claim is true.

findings.problem: Makes an unsourced Greek lexical claim not supplied by the chapter text or book briefing; I believe the claim is true.

findings.guideText: They can represent Law and Prophets, are both associated with Sinai/Horeb revelation, and appear in end-time expectation.

findings.problem: Makes an unsourced Greek etymological and translation-history claim not supplied by the chapter text or book briefing; I believe the claim is true.

findings.evidence: Matthew 17:20 and bookBriefing (neither states that moving mountains was an ancient proverb).
findings.problem: Makes an unsourced historical-linguistic claim about ancient proverbial usage not found in the chapter text or book briefing; I believe the claim is true.

findings.guideText: and likely entered from the parallel tradition in Mark.
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.traditionNote ("later manuscripts expanded the text: for example, some editions include 17:21... while many modern critical-text translations place them in notes", with no mention of Mark).
findings.problem: Makes an unsourced manuscript-history claim that verse 21 entered Matthew from Mark, which neither the chapter text nor the book briefing supplies; I believe the claim is true.

findings.guideText: Jesus reasons that the Son is free in relation to his Father's temple.

findings.problem: Identifies the didrachma collection as a temple tax in relation to the temple without a named source, as neither the chapter text nor the book briefing mentions the temple here; I believe the claim is true.

findings.guideText: Disciples tempted to separate glory, power, and freedom from suffering service

findings.problem: This is an unsourced Greek-language claim not supplied by the grounding; I believe the literal wording claim is true.

findings.guideText: The main command is to make disciples, not merely travel or secure decisions
findings.evidence: Matthew 28:19 (WEB): “Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them…”
findings.problem: A contested grammatical reading of the participles is presented as settled fact without identifying it as a reading or noting that readers differ over the force of “going.”
